changes.new: ### What the graph assumes about labels Semi-supervised smoothness connects nearby outputs along well-supported, high-density regions. The cluster assumption expects one such connected region to contain mostly one class; it does not require every class to form a single cluster. Placing a boundary in a low-density gap avoids splitting that region. These are assumptions about the relation between input density and labels, not consequences of observing unlabelled points. The manifold assumption concerns geometry: high-dimensional inputs may concentrate near a lower-dimensional structure. In the circles example, each curve is one-dimensional even though the coordinates are two-dimensional. Short graph edges can approximate paths along a curve; straight-line distance through empty space need not describe that path. [Chapelle, Schölkopf and Zien, §1.2.1–1.2.3](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~zhuxj/tmp/book.pdf#page=12) distinguish these assumptions. Low-dimensional geometry alone does not supply a class rule. If the intended label changes halfway around one circle, smoothing the same label around the whole curve is wrong. The representation, edge weights and available labels must support the chosen smoothness constraint. ### Harmonic label propagation A hard-clamped harmonic version makes this assumption explicit.

## Noisy Student: clean targets, a noisy learner The iterative self-training procedure above can use two separate models. A teacher first learns from human-labelled examples. It then supplies fixed targets for an unlabelled pool. A student learns from both sources of supervision. After training, that student can become the next teacher, which relabels the pool for another round. [Noisy Student, §2 and Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/html/1911.04252v4#S2) specifies where noise enters this procedure. The teacher generates pseudo-labels in inference mode, on clean inputs, without dropout or stochastic depth. The student learns with input augmentation and model noise. Training the original teacher may itself use regularization; “clean teacher” describes pseudo-label generation, not an assertion that the teacher was trained without noise. The authors' [original Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/1911.04252v4#S2.F1) shows the four stages and puts data augmentation, dropout and stochastic depth beside the student-training stage. The student is equal in size to or larger than the teacher; being smaller is not the method's purpose. A larger architecture provides capacity, not a guarantee that the student will improve. The new teacher is obtained after a training round, rather than by updating an EMA teacher at every minibatch. ### The target remains fixed while the student changes For an unlabelled input $u_i$, let the clean teacher supply the probability vector $q_i$. Let $p_i$ be the student's prediction under its sampled augmentation and model noise. Soft-target cross-entropy is $$ \ell_i=-\sum_c q_{ic}\log p_{ic}. $$ The teacher is held fixed during student training. For student logits $z_i$, the derivative is $p_i-q_i$. If an identical, unnoised student already predicts $p_i=q_i$, this gradient is zero. The cross-entropy value is still $H(q_i)$, not zero unless the target is one-hot. KL divergence would be zero. Noise can make the student's prediction differ from the clean target and create a consistency gradient; it does not make a wrong target correct. The following program compares those cases, then performs one joint student update. Its two-dimensional input changes and dropout isolate the mechanism. They are not RandAugment, stochastic depth, an EfficientNet training run or evidence of improved ImageNet accuracy. ```python import copy import torch import torch.nn.functional as F torch.manual_seed(31) teacher = torch.nn.Sequential( torch.nn.Linear(2, 4), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Dropout(.5), torch.nn.Linear(4, 2) ).double() teacher.eval() student = copy.deepcopy(teacher) u = torch.tensor([[1., .2], [-.8, .4]], dtype=torch.float64) with torch.no_grad(): q = teacher(u).softmax(-1) teacher_before = [p.detach().clone() for p in teacher.parameters()] student.eval() clean_ce = -(q * student(u).log_softmax(-1)).sum(-1).mean() entropy = -(q * q.log()).sum(-1).mean() torch.testing.assert_close(clean_ce.detach(), entropy) assert clean_ce.item() > 0 clean_grad = torch.autograd.grad(clean_ce, tuple(student.parameters())) assert max(g.abs().max().item() for g in clean_grad) < 1e-12 student.train() augmented = u + u.new_tensor([[.4, -.2], [-.3, .1]]) human_x = u.new_tensor([[.6, -.5]]) human_y = torch.tensor([1]) optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(student.parameters(), lr=.1) optimizer.zero_grad() lab = F.cross_entropy(student(human_x), human_y) unl = -(q * student(augmented).log_softmax(-1)).sum(-1).mean() ratio = 2. loss = lab + ratio * unl combined_mean = (lab + 2 * unl) / 3 torch.testing.assert_close(loss, 3 * combined_mean) loss.backward() assert not q.requires_grad assert all(p.grad is None for p in teacher.parameters()) assert any(p.grad is not None and p.grad.norm() > 0 for p in student.parameters()) before = [p.detach().clone() for p in student.parameters()] optimizer.step() assert any(not torch.equal(a, b) for a, b in zip(before, student.parameters())) assert all(torch.equal(a, b) for a, b in zip(teacher_before, teacher.parameters())) print("clean CE / target entropy", clean_ce.item(), entropy.item()) print("labelled / pseudo-labelled losses", lab.item(), unl.item()) ``` Algorithm 1 writes a sum of two dataset means. The released [loss assembly](https://github.com/google-research/noisystudent/blob/aac52bf02448f6e45aee6c418f3e588803e4fa43/main.py) weights the unlabelled mean by its batch-size ratio $r$, giving $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{lab}}+r\mathcal L_{\mathrm{unl}}$ before weight decay. At $r=2$, this is three times the mean over one labelled and two unlabelled examples. The relative supervision weight and overall gradient scale must both be specified. The program uses that reduction and omits the implementation's label smoothing and weight decay. ### Filtering, balancing and another training round The paper's ImageNet protocol starts with roughly 300 million JFT images, whose existing labels are ignored. In [§3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1911.04252v4#S3.SS1), an EfficientNet-B0 filters by confidence above 0.3. At most 130,000 high-confidence images are retained per predicted class; underfilled classes are duplicated to reach the same count. The resulting 130 million training entries contain about 81 million unique images. Pool size, retained entries and unique examples are three different counts. Duplicating a confidently wrong pseudo-label increases its training weight without adding independent evidence. The final iterative run uses B7 as teacher, then L2 as student and as subsequent teacher. [Table 7](https://arxiv.org/html/1911.04252v4#S4) reports 87.6%, 88.1% and 88.4% ImageNet top-1 accuracy across three rounds. The last round also changes the unlabelled-to-labelled batch ratio from 14:1 to 28:1, so its gain cannot be attributed only to replacing the teacher. These are historical vision results, not an NLP benchmark or a universal reason to choose those ratios. For language applications, Luong and Hu's [2021 account of Semi-Supervised Distillation](https://research.google/blog/from-vision-to-language-semi-supervised-learning-in-action-at-scale/) describes a related two-stage procedure: self-train an equal-or-larger teacher, then distil it into a smaller production student. Their SSD variant removes the Noisy Student input-noise requirement for the described Search application. This is a distinct adaptation; it does not establish that the original image augmentations transfer directly to arbitrary NLP tasks. More generally, knowledge distillation can itself use augmentation and regularization, so the presence of noise does not define every distillation method.

## MixText: interpolate hidden states and their targets A back-translation produces another sentence. A convex combination of token identifiers does not: averaging identifiers 10 and 20 gives identifier 15, whose meaning depends on an arbitrary vocabulary order. [Chen, Yang and Yang, §§3–4](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.194/) instead mix continuous encoder states. Their supervised augmentation is called **TMix**. **MixText** adds unlabelled examples, guessed soft labels and further regularization around that operation. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/semi-supervised-extensions-2026-10-29/tmix-original.png|Original TMix hidden-state interpolation and complete caption]] *Jiaao Chen, Zichao Yang and Diyi Yang, [MixText, Figure 1](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.194.pdf#page=1), [CC BY 4.0](https://aclanthology.org/faq/copyright/). Both lower branches use the shared encoder; after mixing, only one branch continues through the upper layers. Complete original figure and caption, rendered at 240 dpi. The PDF's embedded diagram is not enlarged beyond its native pixel dimensions.* ### Where the two encoder branches meet Run both inputs through the same first $m$ layers, obtaining $h_m^a$ and $h_m^b$. Mix their states, then run the mixed state through the remaining layers and classifier: $$ \begin{aligned} \tilde h_m&=\lambda h_m^a+(1-\lambda)h_m^b,\\ \tilde y&=\lambda y_a+(1-\lambda)y_b. \end{aligned} $$ The same coefficient must be used for states and targets. With $h_m^a=(2,0)$, $h_m^b=(0,2)$, $\lambda=0.75$ and opposite one-hot targets, the mixed state is $(1.5,0.5)$ and the target is $(0.75,0.25)$. The upper network predicts a probability distribution and is trained against that soft target. A nonlinear upper network need not already predict the target, or even the weighted average of its two endpoint predictions. The loss encourages the desired interpolation behaviour. The paper samples one coefficient per batch from $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\alpha)$ and folds it with $\lambda\leftarrow\max(\lambda,1-\lambda)$, so the first branch has at least half the weight. Large $\alpha$ concentrates the draw near $1/2$; small $\alpha$ puts more draws near the endpoints, and folding maps either endpoint towards 1. The chosen BERT-base mixing-layer set is $\{7,9,12\}$, sampled per batch. Those layer numbers are an experimental choice for this encoder, not a universal taxonomy of syntax and meaning. The program below uses one state vector per input, a shared trainable lower projection and a nonlinear upper network. If $g$ is the gradient at the mixed state, the two incoming gradients must be $\lambda g$ and $(1-\lambda)g$. Both contribute to the shared lower parameters. ```python import torch import torch.nn.functional as F dtype = torch.float64 lower = torch.eye(2, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) upper = torch.tensor([[1., -.5], [-.7, 1.2]], dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) a, b = torch.tensor([[2., 0.], [0., 2.]], dtype=dtype) ha, hb = lower @ a, lower @ b ha.retain_grad() hb.retain_grad() lam = .75 mixed = lam * ha + (1 - lam) * hb mixed.retain_grad() target = torch.tensor([.75, .25], dtype=dtype) logits = upper @ mixed.tanh() loss = -(target * logits.log_softmax(0)).sum() loss.backward() torch.testing.assert_close(mixed.detach(), mixed.new_tensor([1.5, .5])) torch.testing.assert_close(ha.grad, lam * mixed.grad) torch.testing.assert_close(hb.grad, (1 - lam) * mixed.grad) torch.testing.assert_close(lower.grad, torch.outer(ha.grad, a) + torch.outer(hb.grad, b)) endpoint_probability = ( lam * (upper.detach() @ ha.detach().tanh()).softmax(0) + (1 - lam) * (upper.detach() @ hb.detach().tanh()).softmax(0)) assert not torch.allclose(logits.detach().softmax(0), endpoint_probability) assert lower.grad.norm() > 0 and upper.grad.norm() > 0 print("mixed state / target", mixed.detach().tolist(), target.tolist()) print("mixed prediction / endpoint average", logits.detach().softmax(0).tolist(), endpoint_probability.tolist()) ``` This illustrates an interpolation gradient, not a trained BERT. In a Transformer the mixed tensors contain all token positions, not just the pooled classification vector. Shapes, padding and attention masks must be specified. The released [encoder](https://github.com/SALT-NLP/MixText/blob/f17198d98e1bbb012d8e33cd26e228dd43bb4673/code/mixtext.py) mixes token-state tensors at the selected layer and mean-pools the final sequence. It creates all-ones attention masks when none are supplied. That implementation choice should not be mistaken for a proof that padding can be ignored, or that positions in two unrelated sentences have a token-by-token semantic alignment. ### Guessing a shared target for several views ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/semi-supervised-extensions-2026-10-29/mixtext-original.png|Original complete MixText training framework and caption]] *Chen, Yang and Yang, [MixText, Figure 2](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.194.pdf#page=5), [CC BY 4.0](https://aclanthology.org/faq/copyright/). The red classifier boxes share parameters. Their predictions supply the weighted average and sharpened target; the upper path mixes the resulting labelled and pseudo-labelled pool. Complete original figure and caption, rendered at 240 dpi without redrawing.* For an unlabelled sentence, the paper constructs German and Russian back-translations. Let $p_k$ be predictions on the original and those views, with nonnegative quality weights $w_k$ and positive total weight. The guessed distribution is their weighted mean, followed by sharpening: $$ \begin{aligned} q&=\frac{\sum_k w_kp_k}{\sum_k w_k},\\ \hat q_c&=\frac{q_c^{1/T}}{\sum_jq_j^{1/T}}. \end{aligned} $$ The original and its augmentations receive the same guessed target. They join the human-labelled pool, so TMix can pair labelled inputs with each other, labelled with unlabelled, or two unlabelled inputs. Pseudo-label predictions are detached when used as targets; gradients still train the encoder through the mixed-input branches. For predictions $(0.9,0.1)$, $(0.5,0.5)$ and $(0.1,0.9)$, weights $(1,1,0)$ discard the third view and give $q=(0.7,0.3)$. At $T=0.5$, the sharpened target is $(49/58,9/58)$. Sharpening before averaging would generally give a different distribution. As $T$ tends to zero, probability concentrates on the largest components; a tie does not select a unique one-hot label without an additional tie rule. Lower entropy measures concentration, not correctness. The paper's extra margin term uses the squared probability norm: $$ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{margin}} =\mathbb E_u\max\left(0,\gamma-\sum_c p_c(u)^2\right). $$ For two classes and $\gamma=0.7$, uniform prediction has norm squared $0.5$ and penalty $0.2$; $(0.9,0.1)$ has norm squared $0.82$ and zero penalty. This is not Shannon entropy, even though both can be used to encourage concentration. The probabilities in a trainable penalty need a gradient path. Applying the penalty only to a detached guessed target would not update the learner. ```python import torch dtype = torch.float64 views = torch.tensor([[.9, .1], [.5, .5], [.1, .9]], dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) weight = torch.tensor([1., 1., 0.], dtype=dtype) q = (weight[:, None] * views.detach()).sum(0) / weight.sum() target = q.square() / q.square().sum() torch.testing.assert_close(q, q.new_tensor([.7, .3])) torch.testing.assert_close(target, q.new_tensor([49/58, 9/58])) assert not target.requires_grad logits = torch.tensor([[.5, .5], [.6, .4], [.9, .1]], dtype=dtype).log() logits.requires_grad_() p = logits.softmax(-1) penalties = (.7 - p.square().sum(-1)).clamp_min(0) penalties.mean().backward() torch.testing.assert_close(penalties.detach(), p.new_tensor([.2, .18, 0.])) torch.testing.assert_close(logits.grad[0], torch.zeros(2, dtype=dtype), atol=1e-14, rtol=0) assert logits.grad[1].norm() > 0 and logits.grad[2].count_nonzero() == 0 assert views.grad is None print("guessed / sharpened", q.tolist(), target.tolist()) print("margin penalties / gradients", penalties.detach().tolist(), logits.grad.tolist()) ``` Uniform logits are stationary by symmetry even when this penalty is positive; confidence regularization alone does not resolve which class is correct. Human labels and the remaining objective supply information missing from that symmetric case. ### Paper and released training code are different specifications The pinned [training code](https://github.com/SALT-NLP/MixText/blob/f17198d98e1bbb012d8e33cd26e228dd43bb4673/code/train.py) contains configurable variants. Its current label-guessing expression sets the two translation weights to zero and the original weight to one. Comments give alternative dataset-specific weights; they are not active just because translations were loaded. The usual hidden-mixing branch uses a soft-target cross-entropy on labelled-majority samples and KL on unlabelled-majority samples, with a ramped weight. Cross-entropy and KL have the same prediction gradient for a fixed target but differ by its entropy. The same branch computes a Shannon-entropy hinge, $\max(0,H(p)-\gamma)$, rather than the paper's squared-norm hinge. Moreover, with the default mixing path, the training loop does not add that computed extra term to its loss. Other flags activate different branches. Reproducing a particular run therefore requires its commit, arguments, target weights and actual loss assembly; importing a class named SemiLoss does not determine them. The label-guessing passes run inside no-grad while the model remains in training mode. No-grad stops autograd recording; it does not disable dropout. This is different from Noisy Student's clean inference-mode teacher and should be preserved when comparing implementations. [Table 2 of the ACL paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.194.pdf#page=7) reports these AG News test accuracies with **10 labels per class**: BERT 69.5%, supervised TMix 74.1%, the authors' UDA implementation 84.4%, and MixText 88.4%. AG News has four classes, so that setting uses 40 human labels, not ten in total. The unlabelled pool has 5,000 examples per class. Results are averaged over three runs; the UDA comparison uses the authors' matched PyTorch reimplementation, not UDA's original TPU/BERT-LARGE IMDb protocol. These results do not establish a universal “works below 100 labels” rule across datasets or modern encoders.

### Dai–Le: initialize a sequence classifier before using class labels [Dai and Le, 2015, §§2–4](https://arxiv.org/html/1511.01432v1#S2) compare two ways to initialize an LSTM classifier from unlabelled sequences. A recurrent language model predicts the next token from its prefix. A sequence autoencoder first reads the complete document, then reconstructs that document. Both provide token targets from the stored text, rather than predicting its unknown class label. In the authors' [original Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/1511.01432v1#S2.F1), the input is W, X, Y, Z, followed by an end marker. The recurrent state after that marker starts reconstruction: predict W, consume W and predict X, then Y, Z and the end marker. Encoder and decoder use **the same recurrent weights**. The full document influences the initial decoding state, so this is not the same conditional prediction problem as a language model that has seen only the prefix. The reconstruction must use the finite-dimensional recurrent state; this architecture has no attention path that can retrieve every encoder position directly. | Objective | Inputs available for predicting W | Target supplied by | | --- | --- | --- | | Constructed next-token LM with a start marker | Start marker only | First stored token W | | Sequence reconstruction | W, X, Y, Z and the end marker | First stored token W | | Document classification | The document representation | Human class annotation | For a sequence $x$, the two unsupervised losses can be written as $$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal L_{\mathrm{LM}} &=-\sum_t\log p(x_t\mid x_{ 0 assert body.weight_hh_l0.grad.norm() > 0 optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) # Transfer the trained body, not the vocabulary-output head. class_embedding = copy.deepcopy(embedding) class_body = copy.deepcopy(body) class_head = torch.nn.Linear(5, 2).to(dtype) assert class_body.weight_hh_l0.data_ptr() != body.weight_hh_l0.data_ptr() torch.testing.assert_close(class_body.weight_hh_l0, body.weight_hh_l0) pretrained_snapshot = body.weight_hh_l0.detach().clone() documents = torch.tensor([[2, 3, 4, 5, 1], [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]]) labels = torch.tensor([0, 1]) class_parameters = (list(class_embedding.parameters()) + list(class_body.parameters()) + list(class_head.parameters())) class_optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(class_parameters, lr=.1) class_optimizer.zero_grad() states, _ = class_body(class_embedding(documents)) classification_loss = F.cross_entropy(class_head(states[:, -1]), labels) classification_loss.backward() assert class_embedding.weight.grad.norm() > 0 assert class_body.weight_hh_l0.grad.norm() > 0 assert all(p.grad is None for p in token_head.parameters()) class_optimizer.step() assert not torch.equal(class_body.weight_hh_l0, pretrained_snapshot) assert torch.equal(body.weight_hh_l0, pretrained_snapshot) print("LM / reconstruction losses", lm_loss.item(), sa_loss.item()) print("classification loss", classification_loss.item()) ``` The paper reads complete documents for the reconstruction objective, but uses truncated backpropagation over up to 400 timesteps from the end in the described experiments. Reading the whole sequence does not imply that gradients traverse every earlier step. The nine-step program above does not truncate its graph. The paper's roughly 500,000 pretraining updates, dropout tuning and validation-based early stopping are also absent from this fixture. The experiments distinguish LM-LSTM, SA-LSTM, joint reconstruction plus classification, and linear label gain, which attaches weighted class losses to intermediate timesteps. None is a guarantee that every pretraining objective improves every dataset. For example, their 20 Newsgroups table reports LM-LSTM at 15.3% error and SA-LSTM at 15.6%. The v1 IMDb prose and table disagree on the LM-LSTM number; that internally inconsistent value is not used here as a comparative result. This work demonstrates recurrent parameter initialization followed by supervised fine-tuning. BERT later uses a bidirectional Transformer and masked-token pretraining, whose information access and objective are different. Calling the earlier model “BERT with an LSTM” would hide those differences. The detailed objectives are explained in the linked language-model and BERT chapters above. --- **Предыдущая глава:**
